opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the discussion of AI misalignment risk has historically been framed in a kind of binary way: either we solve alignment, meaning we figure out how to make AI systems that robustly want what we want, or we don't, and then things go catastrophically wrong. I think that framing is pretty unhelpful for figuring out what to actually do over the next few years.

The way I'd rather think about it is that we're probably going to end up in a situation where AI companies are deploying very powerful systems, and they won't have confident evidence that those systems are aligned. Maybe the models are fine, maybe some of them are scheming against us, and we won't be able to tell. That seems like the default trajectory, given how fast things are moving and how immature our alignment techniques and interpretability tools are.

So the question becomes: conditional on being in that messy world, what can we do to reduce the probability that things go badly? That's what I mean by harm reduction. It's analogous to how public health people think about drug use. You'd like nobody to be in a risky situation, but given that people are, you want interventions that make the outcomes less bad.

Concretely, a lot of my work is on what we call AI control: designing protocols for deploying models such that, even if the models are trying to subvert your safety measures, they can't succeed at causing a catastrophe. Things like monitoring model outputs with other models, restricting permissions, auditing suspicious actions, and so on. The nice thing is you don't need to have solved the hard philosophical and technical problem of knowing what's going on inside the model. You just need to be robust to the possibility that it's adversarial.

I emphasize this partly because I think it's tractable. These are relatively cheap, practical interventions that a company with modest political will could actually implement. A lot of the more ambitious proposals require either massive coordination or technical breakthroughs we don't know how to get. And if you think the most likely scenario is that AI developers are going to be somewhat careless and in a hurry, then the interventions that matter most are the ones that still work under those conditions. I'd rather have a plan that reduces risk by a meaningful amount in the world we're likely to be in than a plan that would be great in a world we're probably not going to get.

r001.rationale: The response calls harm-reduction interventions cheap and practical, but does not claim safety researchers give them insufficient attention or mention very limited budgets.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertain assessments where models may be scheming, then argues for deciding what to do in that situation and gives AI control protocols as a plan to reduce risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture is this. I think there's a pretty good chance that at some point in the next decade or so, AI companies are going to be deploying models that are extremely capable, capable enough to do a lot of the work of AI research and a lot of other economically important stuff, and that we won't have the alignment problem solved in any deep sense. We won't be able to look at a model and say with confidence, "This model has the goals we want it to have." And in that world, the question isn't "How do we make sure the model is aligned?" It's "Given that this model might be misaligned and might be actively trying to undermine us, how do we get useful work out of it without things going catastrophically wrong?"

That's what Ryan Greenblatt and I call AI control. And the reason I emphasize it isn't that I think alignment research is bad or hopeless. It's more that it seems like a huge mistake for the whole field to bet everything on a research program that might not pay off in time. If you look at how safety works in other high-stakes domains, like nuclear plants or aviation or insider threats at a bank, nobody says, "We'll just make sure everyone is trustworthy and then we're done." They assume some people might be bad actors and design the system so that a bad actor can't cause a disaster. The bank doesn't rely on only hiring honest tellers. It has audits, dual controls, monitoring. That's the mindset.

And the thing that makes me think this is actually tractable, rather than just a nice analogy, is that the AI labs have an enormous structural advantage over the models they're deploying, at least in the near term. They control what the model sees. They can monitor every action. They can run the model on synthetic inputs where they know the right answer and see whether it behaves. They can use other, possibly weaker, models that they trust more to review the outputs. They can restrict what actions are even possible. And the misaligned model, if it is misaligned, has to succeed at subverting all of that, often without being able to coordinate with other copies of itself and without knowing which situations are real and which are tests. So you can get into a regime where even if the model wants to cause a catastrophe, it doesn't have a good shot at it.

The other thing I'd say is that this framing is just much more amenable to actually being evaluated. If I say "our alignment technique works," it's genuinely hard to know whether that's true, because the failure mode is a model that's deceiving you. But with control, you can run what we call control evaluations, where you have a red team that tries to make the model misbehave within your safety setup, and you measure how often it gets through. That's an empirical question with an answer. You can iterate on it. It feels much more like normal engineering than a lot of alignment work does.

So I guess the short version is: I'm pessimistic that we'll have alignment nailed when we need it, I'm optimistic that control-style measures can buy us a lot of safety in the meantime, and I think the measures are concrete enough that labs could actually implement them. That combination makes it seem like one of the highest-value things to be working on, even though it's a bit less glamorous than solving the problem for real.

r001.rationale: The response advocates AI control alongside alignment research, but does not claim that researchers give this approach insufficient attention or mention very limited budgets.

r002.rationale: It argues that when models may be misaligned, researchers should plan how to use them safely, and describes AI control measures as that response.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that we shouldn’t assume we’ll either solve alignment completely or have no useful options left. There are things we can do to make deploying a potentially misaligned AI less dangerous, even if we haven’t figured out how to make it reliably want what we want.

For example, we can try to limit what systems have access to, monitor their actions, and arrange things so that causing a catastrophe would require getting past several safeguards. None of that is a complete solution. But the question is whether it substantially reduces the probability that a misaligned system can cause harm.

And I think that’s a useful way to frame the problem because it gives us concrete things to work on. Instead of only asking, ‘Can we make this system aligned?’, we can also ask, ‘If this system were trying to undermine us, would we catch it? What could it actually get away with?’ Making progress on those questions seems valuable even while we’re uncertain about how much progress we’ll make on alignment.

r001.rationale: The response advocates practical harm-reduction work, but does not claim that researchers give it insufficient attention or mention limited budgets.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking how a misaligned system could cause harm and how to detect it, but does not say that risk assessments should include a plan for what to do if risk is found or suspected.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s easy to frame AI misalignment as a problem where we either figure out how to make the AI reliably want what we want, or we lose. And I don’t think those are the only possibilities. Even if we can’t be confident that an AI is aligned, we might still be able to make it much harder for that AI to cause a catastrophe.

For example, we can restrict what systems have access to, monitor their actions, and require additional checks before they do something dangerous. None of those measures is a complete solution. But the relevant question is whether, taken together, they substantially reduce the chance that a misaligned system successfully causes harm.

That seems particularly worth working on because we might want to use powerful AI systems to help us solve alignment and other safety problems. So there’s a potentially valuable intermediate state where the systems aren’t trustworthy, but we can use them with enough safeguards to get useful work out of them. I want us to have better options in that situation.

r001.rationale: The response advocates safeguards and harm reduction, but does not claim researchers give this insufficient attention or mention limited budgets.

r002.rationale: It describes safeguards for systems that may be misaligned, but does not connect them to risk-assessment efforts or argue that assessments should include a contingency plan.
